newsitem.title: TAIWAN: FEATURE - Taiwan cracks down on underworld.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Taiwan cracks down on underworld.

text.p: For years, powerful gangsters known collectively as "big brother" have controlled and terrorised Taiwan's political and financial circles.

Mobsters have long wielded power in parliament, sucked kickbacks from major public projects and imposed their will on society with impunity. One even claimed to be a deity and boasted that top politicians worshipped him.
Now, Taiwan's anti-crime tsar says the hoodlums will no longer play god.
After just two months in office, Justice Minister Liao Cheng-hao in August launched an anti-gangster campaign to purge Taiwan's underworld.
"The power of the gangsters is ruining this country, and it is time for law and order to be applied so that people can feel safe again," Liao told Reuters.
By mid-December, the ministry said it had grilled 316 gang members and detained 136 -- including 53 government officials.
But the campaign has so far caused only a gentle ripple in Taiwan's underworld. Police say the island of 21 million people has 10,582 gangsters belonging to 1,236 gangs.
CRACKDOWN SPURRED BY TELEPHONE BIDDING PROCESS
The crackdown has taken on new urgency since Taipei began screening bids for newly liberalised mobile telephone franchises -- projects that are gold mines for gangsters.

Major foreign and domestic firms -- including U.S. giants AT&T Corp and Sprint Corp and Koo's Group of Taiwan -- are vying for the new market which analysts say should be worth US$3.6 billion a year within a decade.
"We will keep a very, very close eye on the entire screening process, because we cannot rule out the possibility that gangsters will try to profit from it," Liao said.
Mobster manipulation has already tainted bidding for public projects ranging from local parks to international airports.
Taipei in April delayed bidding for a T$7 billion (US$257 million) airport terminal construction project after media reported that gangsters had influenced the process.
In September allegations surfaced that gangsters had squeezed healthy kickbacks from bidding for a railway project.
Both projects have been halted pending investigation.
The national Investigation Bureau is probing allegations that gangsters have asserted illegal control over a number of firms listed on the Taiwan Stock Exchange.
POLITICALLY POWERFUL GANGSTERS MAKE PURGE DIFFICULT
National Taiwan University political scientist Tim Ting said preventing infiltration of financial markets was particularly hard because many gangsters held powerful political posts.
"In the past, gangsters tended to stay clear of politics and government. Now, gangsters themselves are trying to take over politics and the government," Ting said.
Minister Liao acknowledges that gangsters have penetrated deep into Taiwan politics and the 162-member parliament, saying Taiwan had the makings of a "new Sicily".
"I would have to say that gangsters' presence in our political system -- including parliament -- is a serious ill and one that will take some time to cure," Liao said.
Parliamentary lawmaker Liao Hsueh-kuang was kidnapped from his home and locked in a kennel overnight at a remote mountain location.
Liao, who police later freed, accused fellow legislator Lo Fu-chu of staging the abduction with members of his gang.
"There are at least 28 to 30 gang members in the parliament right now, and Lo Fu-chu is definitely one of the big shots," Liao said.
Lo has denied any role in the kidnapping, and says Liao is a gang leader. "He (Liao) probably staged the whole kidnap thing himself to get some attention," Lo said.
Taiwan has drafted a bill that bars candidates with records in organised crime from running for political office.
"Right now there are more than 80 registered political parties in Taiwan, and quite frankly a lot of them are gangster organisations trying to legitimise themselves," Liao said.
One gangster took the ultimate high road to legitimacy -- he said he was a god.
For years, Sung Chi-li boasted of possessing miraculous powers and, with his partners, defrauded naive followers of some T$3 billion (US$109 million).

Local media have linked two high-profile politicians -- former vice presidential candidate for main opposition Democratic Progressive Party Frank Hsieh, and Taiwan's deputy police chief Yu Yu-tan -- to Sung's group.
Both Hsieh and Yu have admitted knowing Sung personally, but denied involvement in the scandal.
Sung returned to earth in October, when he was detained by the police and, on failing to demonstrate special powers, admitted to staging the hoax for money.
